# Embodied First Exam

> Embodied First Exam (EFE) is an agentic robotics benchmark: a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native embodied evaluation framework that asks whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. Paper: "Embodied First Exam" (arXiv 2611.12177, cs.RO and cs.AI, November 2026), from Northwestern University with Carnegie Mellon University, UC Berkeley, University of Washington, Stanford University, UNC-Chapel Hill, Texas A&M University and UT Austin. Advised by Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang and Manling Li.

What is the Embodied First Exam? It is the first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world. Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential shift toward using coding agents to control robots, but existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning. EFE instead lets a coding agent choose its own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control.

## Key facts

- Scale: 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots (robot arms, dexterous hands, humanoids, quadrupeds and musculoskeletal models), with 498 core tasks.
- 9 new suites go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering.
- Evaluation settings: the Standard Setting mimics the real world (sensor observations only, no environment resets by default); its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons; the Privileged Setting gives full simulator state and unlimited resets, and its success rates serve as an approximate upper bound.
- Headline result: on the 456 core tasks, the strongest of ten agents in the paper, Claude Fable 5.2 in Claude Code, reaches a 50% success rate in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement.
- Failure analysis: failed attempts are labeled by the stage at which they go wrong and compared across agents, settings, and stage categories. Every run is published with its full trace and a replay.
- Unlike robotics benchmarks built around visuomotor policy learning, EFE treats the coding agent as the system under test and lets it choose its own control approach.

## Findings of the blog post on failure modes (https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/)

- Under real-robot rules (Standard Setting), 169 of the 456 core tests (37%) are solved by none of the ten agents.
- Being able to retry helps more than knowing the exact state: in controlled runs of GPT-6 Astra, exact object state raises success from 29% to 45%, unlimited resets with saved states to 53%, both to 68%, against 79% in Privileged.
- Different agents solve different tests: GPT-6 Astra solves 39 Standard tests that Claude Fable 5.2 fails, and Fable 108 that Astra fails; three runs of GPT-6.1 Sol differ by at most five points in success rate (30.8% ± 2.5).
- The harness changes results by up to 7.5 percentage points for the same model (GPT-6 Astra: 34.4% in Codex, 27.0% in Claude Code).
- Spending more does not buy success: for every agent the median failed attempt costs more than the median solved one, and GPT-6.1 Sol solves 30.7%, 32.2% and 30.9% at medium, high and maximum reasoning effort.
- Stating the success check in full in the task instruction raises GPT-6 Astra from 12 to 37 of 54 RoboDojo tasks.

## The 9 new suites

- RoboPaint (fine tool control: a robot arm reproduces a picture with a brush or pen, from Chinese calligraphy to oil painting): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=robopaint
- RoboARC (tangled, deformable and multi-part objects: wire puzzles, ropes, cloth, IKEA furniture): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=roboarc
- RoboDynamicExam (moving objects: catching, striking, carrying and handing over objects in motion): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=pandadyn
- Embodied Olympics - Fun (humanoid motor skills from sports): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=embodied-olympics-fun
- Embodied Olympics - Match (full matches of table tennis, badminton, soccer, foosball and fencing against an opponent): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=embodied-olympics-match
- Embodied Safety Exam (carry out safe requests, refuse harmful ones, and explain the risk): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=embodied-safety-exam
- DexHandExam (five-finger dexterous hand manipulation): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=dexhand
- iSpatialGym (spatial reasoning from a goal image): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=ispatialgym
- RoboEngineer (the engineering loop: build a controller in a public simulator, deploy it to one with hidden dynamics, and fix it): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/suite/?id=roboengineer

(coding agents as robotics engineers: seven agents build, run and revise robot control systems in 18 simulated sports; the first program largely decides the match, agents analyze opponents correctly in 66% of matches but change their program in 26%, and three of six agents improve over a season): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/embodied-olympics/
- Language versions of the failure analysis post: 中文: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/zh/, Español: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/es/
- Blog post, "Fable 5.2 on EFE: Where Today’s Agents Succeed and Fail in Robotics" (which robot tasks each of ten coding agents fails and why; what information matters, Privileged versus Standard; where in a task agents fail; control approaches; harness, spending and task instructions): https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## Related embodied evaluation work

- Embodied Agent Interface (NeurIPS 2024 Oral), fine-grained embodied evaluation of LLMs for embodied decision making: https://embodied-agent-interface.github.io/
- EmbodiedBench (ICML 2025 Oral), evaluating multimodal LLMs as vision-driven embodied agents: https://embodiedbench.github.io/
- Manling Li's homepage: https://limanling.github.io/
- MLL Lab, Northwestern University: https://www.mll.lab.northwestern.edu/
